tooltip.title: Clinical Approach
tooltip.markdown: Following the logical thought process of a clinician evaluating a patient with hair loss.

tooltip.title: History Taking
tooltip.markdown: The cornerstone of the evaluation. Details gathered here will guide the physical exam and diagnostic testing.

tooltip.title: Timeline & Onset
tooltip.markdown:
-   **Acute vs. Chronic:** Sudden onset suggests Telogen Effluvium or Alopecia Areata. Gradual onset suggests Androgenetic Alopecia or a scarring process.
-   **Duration:** How long has the patient been experiencing hair loss?
-   **Triggers:** Inquire about recent illness (esp. febrile), surgery, major life stress, or starting new medications.

tooltip.title: Scalp Symptoms
tooltip.markdown:
-   **Significance:** The presence of itching, burning, pain, or pustules strongly suggests an active inflammatory process.
-   **Associated Conditions:** Common in Lichen Planopilaris, Folliculitis Decalvans, and Discoid Lupus. Less common but can occur in Alopecia Areata.

tooltip.title: Medication History
tooltip.markdown:
-   **Importance:** A wide range of medications can induce Telogen Effluvium. It is critical to get a full list of prescription, OTC, and supplement use.
-   **Examples:** Retinoids, anticoagulants, beta-blockers, and some biologics are known culprits.

tooltip.title: Medical & Gynecological History
tooltip.markdown:
-   **Systemic Clues:** Ask about thyroid disease, autoimmune conditions (lupus, vitiligo), and signs of hyperandrogenism (acne, hirsutism).
-   **Hormonal Factors:** Inquire about menstrual regularity and history of PCOS, pregnancy, or menopause.

tooltip.title: Hair Care Habits
tooltip.markdown:
-   **Mechanical Stress:** High-tension styles (tight braids, ponytails, weaves) can cause Traction Alopecia.
-   **Chemical/Heat Damage:** Frequent use of relaxers, perms, bleach, or high-heat styling tools can lead to hair shaft breakage.

tooltip.title: Physical Examination
tooltip.markdown: A detailed examination of the scalp and hair is performed to identify the pattern of loss and specific clinical signs.

tooltip.title: Pattern of Hair Loss
tooltip.markdown:
-   **Androgenetic:** Bitemporal recession and vertex thinning in men (MPHL); central part widening in women (FPHL).
-   **Patchy:** Well-demarcated round patches are classic for Alopecia Areata.
-   **Diffuse:** Generalized thinning seen in Telogen Effluvium.

tooltip.title: The Critical Question: Scarring?
tooltip.markdown: The most important branch point in the diagnostic algorithm. The presence of scarring signifies permanent follicular destruction.

tooltip.title: Follicular Ostia (Pores)
tooltip.markdown: Loss of follicular openings supports established cicatricial alopecia. Visible ostia do not exclude early inflammatory scarring disease; correlate symptoms, perifollicular changes, trichoscopy, and biopsy when indicated.

tooltip.title: Associated Inflammatory Signs
tooltip.markdown: Erythema (redness), scale, and pustules around the hair follicles are clues for an active scarring alopecia like LPP or DLE.

tooltip.title: Hair Shaft Examination
tooltip.markdown: Assess for breakage, which can be the primary cause of apparent hair loss.

tooltip.title: Hair Pull Test
tooltip.markdown: Gently pull a small bundle of hairs and document site, technique, and number removed. The historical >10% cutoff is not universal: a study of 181 healthy participants found 97.2% had two or fewer hairs removed. An increased result supports active shedding but does not identify its cause.

tooltip.title: Associated Physical Signs
tooltip.markdown: Check for signs of systemic disease, such as nail pitting in alopecia areata or skin rashes in lupus erythematosus.
